# Control plane retry matrix

<!-- generated by `quantick-app --dump-retry-matrix`; do not edit -->

What a client does when a call that changes something did not answer:
read the state back unless cancellation proved it never started. One row
per mutable capability the running application registers; read-only
capabilities change nothing and need no reconciling.

This file is generated; a hand edit is a guard failure, not a correction.
Each row lives beside the capability it reconciles, in that family's own
module under `crates/control-schema/src/` — the drawings in `analysis.rs`,
the ticket in `trade.rs` — and `retry_matrix::rows::FAMILIES` is the list
that joins them. The generator refuses to render while any row disagrees
with the registry. To change a row, change it in its family module, or
change the capability, and regenerate:

```sh
cargo run -p quantick-app -- --dump-retry-matrix \
  > docs/control-plane/retry-matrix.md
```

`cargo test -p quantick-app retry_matrix` compares this file with the
generator and every row with the registry; `cargo test -p quantick-guards`
compares it with the [capability inventory](capability-inventory.md) in a
second.

## Reading a row

**Versions** lists every registered version of the capability; the row
holds for all of them, and **Policy** and **Reach** are the newest's. Call
the newest: a version is added when the previous one's contract had to
change, and the older one is kept only so an existing client does not
break.

**Policy** is the `idempotency` the descriptor publishes. **Enforced** is
what the gateway does with it:

- *deduplicated per connection* — a call carrying an idempotency key is
  recorded against the connection that made it. The same key with the same
  input answers the first call's recorded outcome without acting again; the
  same key with different input is `control.idempotency_conflict`; a retry
  that arrives while the first call is still running is
  `control.request_in_progress` (non-retryable; reconcile). A call the
  application began and had still not answered a full request window after
  its deadline records a non-retryable `control.timeout` whose next step is
  to read the state back: its outcome is unknown, and retrying the key cannot
  learn it.
- *key refused; not retryable, read back* — a call carrying a key is
  refused before dispatch (`control.invalid_request`). Sending the call
  twice acts twice, so a client whose call did not answer reads the state
  back instead.
- *refused before dispatch: no grant reaches it* — the capability's
  ceiling is one no grant hands out, so no connection can call it, keyed or
  not. The row records what its readback will be when that changes.

**Reach** is the lowest profile whose ceiling admits the capability.
Every readback is readable by a connection granted the capability's own
permissions and the default read grant (the generator refuses a row that
is not), so reconciling never needs a scope the trader did not already
tick for the call. A capability no grant reaches is held to its ceiling
instead, and its row says which further scope its readback needs.
**Readback** is the read that shows the effect — a `snapshot.read` scope,
or `events.read` filtered to one journal event kind — and **Field** the
path within it, `[]` stepping into an array. **Applied when** says what the
field shows if the call took effect. **Proven by** names the transport
tests, in `crates/app/src/app/tests/retry_readback_tests.rs`, that exercise
the row through the real local gateway.

To reconcile, take the reading *before* the call — the scope's value, or
an `events.read` cursor at `latest` — and compare it with the same read
afterwards. A snapshot read can be retried freely: reads are read-only.

## The guarantee ends with the connection

Deduplication is scoped to the connection that made the call. A client
that reconnects arrives as a new principal, and its keys are new keys: the
same key re-executes rather than replaying. That is deliberate — the only
identities that survive a reconnect are the bearer token, which every
client of one grant shares, and a client-supplied name nothing
authenticates, and scoping records by either would let one client replay
another's answer. Widening it needs a durable client identity the
handshake proves, which is a contract change tracked in
[#362](https://github.com/milocaetano/quantick/issues/362). Until then a
client whose connection dropped with a call in flight reconciles *every*
row — `optional` ones included — through its readback, never by retrying
the key on the new connection.

## Missing replies and retry advice

A mutation that may have started returns `retryable: false` and
`details.outcome: unknown` on deadline. A gateway cancellation that wins
before dispatch returns `details.outcome: not_started` and can be retried;
the cancelled request cannot later act. A key deduplicates while its
reservation or terminal record is retained, but another principal's
traffic can evict that record before its TTL; a missing result therefore
requires readback even with a key. Transport loss is non-retryable for every
mutation, including keyed calls. Read the row below to reconcile.
An oversized terminal result retains a compact non-retryable uncertainty
refusal under its key instead of allowing another execution.

`quantick_invoke` accepts an optional `idempotency_key` (1 to 128 printable
ASCII bytes) and passes it unchanged in the request envelope. The runtime
enforces the row's key policy. The MCP adapter learns read-only retry
classification from the runtime registry; unknown metadata is conservative.

Real post-start deadline and post-execution socket-loss proofs live in
`crates/app/src/app/tests/mutation_uncertainty_tests.rs`; adapter-to-wire
key and lost-reply proofs live in `crates/mcp/tests/fake_gateway.rs`.

| **Total** | **130** |
